claim: Humanized and non-humanized NSG mice infected with B. burgdorferi developed progressive inflammation starting in the infected ankle joint followed by swelling of the contralateral non-infected joint.
source: As shown in Figure 1A and B both, non-humanized and humanized mice developed progressive inflammation starting in the infected (right foot) ankle joint followed by swelling of the contralateral non-infected (left foot) joint.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and B, which presents measurements of joint inflammation in infected mice.

claim: Joint inflammation of both paws was strongly delayed in humanized mice compared to non-humanized mice.
source: If mice were humanized, however, joint inflammation of both paws was strongly delayed, suggesting that the human immune system participates in limiting pathogen burden.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations comparing humanized and non-humanized mice, with data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: One week after infection of humanized mice, B. burgdorferi was largely confined to the infected joint and detectable in the blood of about half of the animals.
source: While one week after infection of humanized mice B. burgdorferi was still largely confined to the infected joint (and in about half of the animals detectable in the blood), two weeks after infection bacterial spread to the blood, heart and ears became detectable.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements of pathogen distribution in infected humanized mice at different time points.

claim: Two weeks after infection, bacterial spread to the blood, heart and ears became detectable in humanized mice.
source: While one week after infection of humanized mice B. burgdorferi was still largely confined to the infected joint (and in about half of the animals detectable in the blood), two weeks after infection bacterial spread to the blood, heart and ears became detectable.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data tracking pathogen distribution over time.

claim: Around 5 weeks after infection, B. burgdorferi was very prominent in skin (ears) and in the left foot.
source: Around 5 weeks after infection, B. burgdorferi was very prominent in skin (ears) and in the left foot (Figure 1C,D), consistent with the initiation of inflammation in the contralateral joint (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1C and 1D measuring pathogen load in different tissues.

claim: Humanized mice developed a human IgM response directed against a variety of B. burgdorferi antigens including p39 and OspC.
source: Concomitant with the infection, humanized mice developed a human IgM response directed against a variety of B. burgdorferi antigens including p39 and the outer surface protein C (OspC), which was comparable to the IgM response detectable in B. burgdorferi infected patients (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1E comparing antibody responses in humanized mice and human patients.

claim: The IgM response in humanized mice was comparable to the IgM response detectable in B. burgdorferi infected patients.
source: Concomitant with the infection, humanized mice developed a human IgM response directed against a variety of B. burgdorferi antigens including p39 and the outer surface protein C (OspC), which was comparable to the IgM response detectable in B. burgdorferi infected patients (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative western blot data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Human and mouse immune cell infiltrates, consisting of mouse neutrophils and human myeloid cells, B cells, and CD4+ and CD8+ T cells could be detected in the joints of infected mice.
source: Furthermore, human and mouse immune cell infiltrates, consisting of mouse neutrophils and human myeloid cells, B cells, and CD4+ and CD8+ T cells could be detected in the joints of infected mice (Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2 and supplementary figures.

claim: T cells and B cells showed an activated phenotype in the joints compared to the blood, identified by increased expression of CD69.
source: Compared to the blood, especially T cells and B cells showed an activated phenotype, identified by increased expression of CD69 (Figure 2B,C,H,I,K,L).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data measuring CD69 expression shown in Figure 2.

claim: No major change in serum complement C3 levels was observed during the course of infection.
source: In contrast, no major change in serum complement C3 levels was observed during the course of infection (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA measurements of complement C3 shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Cells of the human innate and adaptive immune system respond to the infection with B. burgdorferi in humanized mice in vivo.
source: In summary, these results suggest that cells of the human innate and adaptive immune system respond to the infection with B. burgdorferi and may help in limiting pathogen burden in humanized mice in vivo.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing immune cell infiltration and activation in infected humanized mice.

claim: The human immune system may help in limiting pathogen burden in humanized mice in vivo.
source: In summary, these results suggest that cells of the human innate and adaptive immune system respond to the infection with B. burgdorferi and may help in limiting pathogen burden in humanized mice in vivo.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the observed delayed joint inflammation in humanized versus non-humanized mice.

claim: The transient depletion of B cells with Rituximab resulted in a long-term reduction of B cells in humanized mice without infection.
source: While this 1-week cycle of B cell depletion resulted in a long-term reduction of B cells in humanized mice without infection, in infected animals peripheral blood B cell counts started to increase after stopping Rituximab injection and reached pre-depletion levels within 3 weeks (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data tracking B cell numbers shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In infected animals, peripheral blood B cell counts started to increase after stopping Rituximab injection and reached pre-depletion levels within 3 weeks.
source: While this 1-week cycle of B cell depletion resulted in a long-term reduction of B cells in humanized mice without infection, in infected animals peripheral blood B cell counts started to increase after stopping Rituximab injection and reached pre-depletion levels within 3 weeks (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The reduction of serum IgM and impaired production of B. burgdorferi-specific antibodies was maintained over 4 weeks after B cell depletion therapy.
source: In contrast to the rapid recovery of peripheral blood B cells, the reduction of serum IgM and impaired production of B. burgdorferi-specific antibodies was maintained over 4 weeks and only started to recover around 5 weeks post B cell depletion therapy (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data measuring serum IgM and pathogen-specific antibodies shown in Figures 3C and 3D.

claim: Autoreactive B cell responses against glucose 6-phosphate isomerase (GPI) and double-stranded DNA were initiated during the course of B. burgdorferi infection.
source: Of note, we also detected the initiation of autoreactive B cell responses against glucose 6-phosphate isomerase (GPI) and double-stranded DNA during the course of B. burgdorferi infection (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data measuring autoantibodies shown in Figures 3E and 3F.

claim: Autoreactive antibody responses were diminished in parallel to the suppression of the B. burgdorferi-specific antibody response by Rituximab treatment.
source: In parallel to the suppression of the B. burgdorferi-specific antibody response by Rituximab treatment, autoreactive antibody responses were diminished.
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data comparing antibody responses in Rituximab-treated and control mice shown in Figures 3D, 3E, and 3F.

claim: Two weeks after infection, 60% of B cell depleted animals tested positive for B. burgdorferi in ear tissue, compared to only 30% of animals with a functional B cell compartment.
source: Thus, 2 weeks after infection 60% of B cell depleted animals tested positive for B. burgdorferi in ear tissue, compared to only 30% of animals with a functional B cell compartment (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: The pathogen load in ears and in the heart was reduced in non B-cell depleted animals compared to B cell depleted animals until the end of the experiment.
source: Moreover, the pathogen load in ears and in the heart was reduced compared to non B-cell depleted animals until the end of the experiment (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: The transient reduction in the humoral immune response resulted in a mild increase of joint swelling especially of the non-infected joint 4 to 5 weeks after infection.
source: With respect to joint inflammation, the transient reduction in the humoral immune response resulted in a mild increase of joint swelling especially of the non-infected joint 4 to 5 weeks after infection (Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by joint thickness measurements shown in Figure 3G.

claim: CD4+ T cell depletion with a CD4-specific antibody resulted in a strong reduction of CD4 T cells throughout the experiment.
source: While this resulted in a strong reduction of CD4 T cells throughout the experiment, it had no impact on the production of pathogen-specific IgM antibodies, suggesting that mostly T cell independent antibody responses were critical for controlling B. burgdorferi infection in humanized mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: CD4+ T cell depletion had no impact on the production of pathogen-specific IgM antibodies.
source: While this resulted in a strong reduction of CD4 T cells throughout the experiment, it had no impact on the production of pathogen-specific IgM antibodies, suggesting that mostly T cell independent antibody responses were critical for controlling B. burgdorferi infection in humanized mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Mostly T cell independent antibody responses were critical for controlling B. burgdorferi infection in humanized mice.
source: While this resulted in a strong reduction of CD4 T cells throughout the experiment, it had no impact on the production of pathogen-specific IgM antibodies, suggesting that mostly T cell independent antibody responses were critical for controlling B. burgdorferi infection in humanized mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B,C).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that CD4 T cell depletion did not affect pathogen-specific antibody production.

claim: CD4+ T cell depletion had no impact on progression of arthritis.
source: In addition to and in agreement with a previous study, CD4+ T cell depletion neither had an impact on progression of arthritis (not shown) (Lasky et al., 2016) nor on pathogen load (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations and cited literature (Lasky et al., 2016).

claim: CD4+ T cell depletion had no impact on pathogen load.
source: In addition to and in agreement with a previous study, CD4+ T cell depletion neither had an impact on progression of arthritis (not shown) (Lasky et al., 2016) nor on pathogen load (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: The early T-cell-independent humoral immune system plays an important role in limiting B. burgdorferi replication and pathogen induced pathology in humanized mice.
source: Altogether, this set of experiments suggests that the early T-cell-independent humoral immune system plays an important role in limiting B. burgdorferi replication and pathogen induced pathology in humanized mice.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined results of B cell and CD4 T cell depletion experiments.

claim: Humanized mice with the non-functional FcγRIIb allele showed a clearly detectable expansion of CD138+ plasma blasts in the blood.
source: As demonstrated in Figure 4A and B, humanized mice with the non-functional FcγRIIb allele showed a clearly detectable expansion of CD138+ plasma blasts in the blood, whereas plasma blasts did not increase in mice with the functional FcγRIIb allele.
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figures 4A and 4B.

claim: Plasma blasts did not increase in mice with the functional FcγRIIb allele.
source: As demonstrated in Figure 4A and B, humanized mice with the non-functional FcγRIIb allele showed a clearly detectable expansion of CD138+ plasma blasts in the blood, whereas plasma blasts did not increase in mice with the functional FcγRIIb allele.
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figures 4A and 4B.

claim: Plasma blast expansion in humanized mice with the non-functional FcγRIIb allele occurred in two separate waves peaking at 1 and 4 weeks after infection.
source: Moreover, plasma blast expansion in humanized mice with the non-functional FcγRIIb allele occurred in two separate waves peaking at 1 and 4 weeks after infection (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: A stronger increase in serum IgM and B. burgdorferi-specific IgM responses was detectable in FcγRIIb-232T humanized mice.
source: In line with the increased level of plasma blasts in FcγRIIb-232T humanized mice, a stronger increase in serum IgM and B. burgdorferi-specific IgM responses was detectable in these animals (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figures 4C and 4D.

claim: Pathogen load in ears was reduced in FcγRIIb-232T humanized mice 2 weeks after infection.
source: In line with the stronger humoral immune response, pathogen load in ears was reduced in FcγRIIb-232T humanized mice 2 weeks after infection (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B) and this reduced pathogen burden was maintained until the end of the experiment (day 35 after infection) (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: The reduced pathogen burden in FcγRIIb-232T humanized mice was maintained until the end of the experiment (day 35 after infection).
source: In line with the stronger humoral immune response, pathogen load in ears was reduced in FcγRIIb-232T humanized mice 2 weeks after infection (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B) and this reduced pathogen burden was maintained until the end of the experiment (day 35 after infection) (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative PCR data shown in Figures 4E and 4F.

claim: A stronger development of self-reactive antibodies directed against double stranded DNA and GPI was observed in humanized mice with the non-functional FcγRIIb-232T allele compared to the functional FcγRIIb allele.
source: However, compared to the functional FcγRIIb allele, a stronger development of self-reactive antibodies directed against double stranded DNA and GPI could be observed in humanized mice with the non-functional FcγRIIb-232T allele (Figure 4G,H).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data measuring autoantibodies shown in Figures 4G and 4H.

claim: FcγRIIb function is critical to limit the production of autoreactive antibodies during an immune response against B. burgdorferi.
source: In summary, these results suggest that FcγRIIb function is critical to limit the production of autoreactive antibodies during an immune response against B. burgdorferi.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison of autoantibody responses in humanized mice with functional versus non-functional FcγRIIb alleles.

claim: The induction of increased serum IgM levels in humanized mice upon B. burgdorferi infection coincided with the appearance of pathogen specific but also self-reactive immune responses.
source: This analysis confirmed that the induction of increased serum IgM levels in humanized mice upon B. burgdorferi infection coincided with the appearance of pathogen specific but also self-reactive immune responses (Figures 5A,B and 4G,H).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis of antibody responses shown in Figures 5A and 5B.

claim: A clear correlation between the induction of B. burgdorferi and GPI-specific antibody responses became evident across all time points and levels of reactivity.
source: When further plotting B. burgdorferi-specific immune responses of individual mice against DNA and GPI-specific autoantibody responses a clear correlation between the induction of B. burgdorferi and GPI-specific antibody responses became evident across all time points and levels of reactivity, while only those animals producing the highest levels of pathogen-specific antibodies also produced antibodies directed against DNA (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figures 5C and 5D.

claim: Only those animals producing the highest levels of pathogen-specific antibodies also produced antibodies directed against DNA.
source: When further plotting B. burgdorferi-specific immune responses of individual mice against DNA and GPI-specific autoantibody responses a clear correlation between the induction of B. burgdorferi and GPI-specific antibody responses became evident across all time points and levels of reactivity, while only those animals producing the highest levels of pathogen-specific antibodies also produced antibodies directed against DNA (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figures 5C and 5D.

claim: B. burgdorferi-specific IgM responses showed a strong correlation with the induction of GPI-specific antibody responses in the patient cohort but not in the healthy control cohort.
source: In striking similarity to the results in humanized mice, B. burgdorferi-specific IgM responses showed a strong correlation with the induction of GPI-specific antibody responses in the patient but not in the healthy control cohort (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis of human patient and control samples shown in Figures 6A and 6B.

claim: The correlation between B. burgdorferi-specific IgM responses and DNA-specific immune response was much less pronounced in human patients, similar to the observations in humanized mice.
source: In contrast, the correlation with the DNA-specific immune response was much less pronounced, similar to the observations in humanized mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis of human patient samples shown in Figure 6B.

claim: All patients in the cohort were homozygous for the functional FcγRIIb-232I allele.
source: Unfortunately (but not unexpectedly), all of the patients in our cohort were homozygous for the functional FcγRIIb-232I allele, not allowing to study the impact of a loss of FcγRIIb function during B. burgdorferi infection in humans.
evidence: The claim is based on genotyping data of the patient cohort.

claim: There is a clear correlation between the induction of pathogen-specific and autoreactive antibody responses, which is regulated by the human inhibitory FcγRIIb at least in humanized mice.
source: Nonetheless, our results suggest that there is a clear correlation between the induction of pathogen-specific and autoreactive antibody responses, which is regulated by the human inhibitory FcγRIIb at least in humanized mice.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined results in humanized mice and human patients.

claim: The spread of B. burgdorferi and the pathogen induced pathology in immunodeficient mouse strains mimics many features of the human disease.
source: We used a model of B. burgdorferi infection, as the spread of the pathogen and the pathogen induced pathology in immunodeficient mouse strains mimics many features of the human disease (Steere and Glickstein, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Steere and Glickstein, 2004).

claim: NSG mice develop an inflammation of the infected joint, followed by systemic pathogen spread and a delayed arthritis of distant joints during later stages of infection with B. burgdorferi.
source: Consistent with previous studies using Borrelia hermsii, we demonstrate that NSG mice develop an inflammation of the infected joint, followed by systemic pathogen spread and a delayed arthritis of distant joints during later stages of infection with B. burgdorferi (Barthold et al., 1990; Vuyyuru et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and cited literature (Barthold et al., 1990; Vuyyuru et al., 2011).

claim: Human B cells, T cells and myeloid cells infiltrated the infected joints and showed a highly activated phenotype, similar to observations in human patients with Lyme arthritis.
source: Indeed, human B cells, T cells and myeloid cells infiltrated the infected joints and showed a highly activated phenotype, similar to observations in human patients with Lyme arthritis (Gross et al., 1998; Yssel et al., 1991).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and cited literature (Gross et al., 1998; Yssel et al., 1991).

claim: The human T helper cell independent humoral immune response was dominantly involved in limiting B. burgdorferi pathology.
source: As removal of B cells but not CD4+T cells impaired pathogen control, the human T helper cell independent humoral immune response was dominantly involved in limiting B. burgdorferi pathology, in line with previous results in inbred mouse strains (Barthold et al., 1996; Barthold et al., 2006; LaRocca and Benach, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and cited literature (Barthold et al., 1996; Barthold et al., 2006; LaRocca and Benach, 2008).

claim: The humanized mouse model of B. burgdorferi infection recapitulates important aspects of the human infection.
source: Altogether this supports the notion that the humanized mouse model of B. burgdorferi infection recapitulates important aspects of the human infection, allowing to investigate how the human inhibitory FcγRIIb controls the humoral immune response during infection in vivo.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined experimental observations comparing humanized mice to human patients.

claim: Human FcγRIIb is a critical regulator of the magnitude and quality of the human immune response in humanized mice.
source: By comparing the immune response in humanized mice with functional (FcγRIIb-232I) and non-functional (FcγRIIb-232T) FcγRIIb alleles side by side, our results suggest that human FcγRIIb indeed is a critical regulator of the magnitude and quality of the human immune response in humanized mice.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison of immune responses in humanized mice with different FcγRIIb alleles.

claim: In the presence of the non-functional FcγRIIb-232T allele, a lower pathogen burden in the directly infected joint and in the skin, heart and distal joint was observed.
source: Thus, in the presence of the non-functional FcγRIIb-232T allele, a lower pathogen burden in the directly infected joint and in the skin, heart and distal joint was observed.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative PCR data measuring pathogen load in different tissues.

claim: A broader panel of naïve B cells may become activated and develop into plasma blasts in the absence of FcγRIIb function.
source: Firstly, a broader panel of naïve B cells may become activated and develop into plasma blasts in the absence of FcγRIIb function, as has been observed in FcγRIIb-deficient mice (Nakamura et al., 2003; Takai et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from cited literature on FcγRIIb-deficient mice (Nakamura et al., 2003; Takai et al., 1996).

claim: The increased appearance of autoantibodies in FcγRIIb-232T humanized mice coincided with the second wave of plasma blasts.
source: Interestingly, the increased appearance of autoantibodies in FcγRIIb-232T humanized mice coincided with the second wave of plasma blasts, whereas increased levels of pathogen-specific immune responses were detectable much earlier.
evidence: The claim is based on temporal analysis of antibody responses and plasma blast expansion shown in Figure 4.

claim: Increased levels of pathogen-specific immune responses were detectable much earlier than the increased appearance of autoantibodies in FcγRIIb-232T humanized mice.
source: Interestingly, the increased appearance of autoantibodies in FcγRIIb-232T humanized mice coincided with the second wave of plasma blasts, whereas increased levels of pathogen-specific immune responses were detectable much earlier.
evidence: The claim is based on temporal analysis of antibody responses shown in Figure 4.

claim: The continued presence of the pathogen may increase the likelihood to develop secondary autoreactive immune responses if FcγRIIb function is missing.
source: These results may indicate that either the continued presence of the pathogen increases the likelihood to develop secondary autoreactive immune responses if FcγRIIb function is missing; or, that the induction of autoantibody responses is developing in parallel but at a reduced strength.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the temporal pattern of autoantibody development.

claim: The induction of autoantibody responses may be developing in parallel to pathogen-specific responses but at a reduced strength.
source: These results may indicate that either the continued presence of the pathogen increases the likelihood to develop secondary autoreactive immune responses if FcγRIIb function is missing; or, that the induction of autoantibody responses is developing in parallel but at a reduced strength.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the temporal pattern of autoantibody development.

claim: Lack of FcγRIIb function on human DCs present in humanized mice may contribute to the induction of autoreactive immune responses by lowering the threshold for DC activation and (auto)antigen presentation.
source: It is important to note that in this scenario lack of FcγRIIb function on human DCs present in humanized mice may also contribute to the induction of autoreactive immune responses, by lowering the threshold for DC activation and (auto)antigen presentation (Desai et al., 2007; Dhodapkar et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference and cited literature (Desai et al., 2007; Dhodapkar et al., 2005).

claim: FcγRIIb on DCs participates in presenting intact antigen to B cells.
source: Furthermore, FcγRIIb on DCs was shown to participate in presenting intact antigen to B cells, which may be another pathway along which DCs contribute to the induction of humoral immune responses in humanized mice (Bergtold et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature (Bergtold et al., 2005).

claim: FcγRIIb cross-linking on plasma cells residing in the bone marrow triggers plasma cell apoptosis, allowing newly formed plasma cells to access survival niches in the bone marrow.
source: Secondly, FcγRIIb cross-linking on plasma cells residing in the bone marrow was shown to trigger plasma cell apoptosis, allowing newly formed plasma cells to access survival niches in the bone marrow (Xiang et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature (Xiang et al., 2007).

claim: In the absence of FcγRIIb function, more plasma blasts/cells may accumulate in the periphery due to a reduced level of plasma cell apoptosis in the bone marrow.
source: Thus, in the absence of FcγRIIb function more plasma blasts/cells may accumulate in the periphery due to a reduced level of plasma cell apoptosis in the bone marrow.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from cited literature on FcγRIIb function in plasma cells.

claim: In humans, the non-functional FcγRIIb allele is enriched in regions with malaria and protects from certain cerebral forms of the disease, while simultaneously increasing the risk to develop autoimmune diseases.
source: Overall, our results are consistent with reports demonstrating that in humans the non-functional FcγRIIb allele is enriched in regions with malaria and protects from certain cerebral forms of the disease, while simultaneously increasing the risk to develop autoimmune diseases (Clatworthy et al., 2007; Waisberg et al., 2011; Willcocks et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature (Clatworthy et al., 2007; Waisberg et al., 2011; Willcocks et al., 2010).

claim: The GPI-specific immune response showed a clear correlation with the induction of B. burgdorferi-specific antibodies.
source: Indeed, especially the GPI-specific immune response showed a clear correlation with the induction of B. burgdorferi-specific antibodies, while the DNA-specific autoantibody responses mostly correlated in mice with a very high antibody response.
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: The DNA-specific autoantibody responses mostly correlated in mice with a very high antibody response.
source: Indeed, especially the GPI-specific immune response showed a clear correlation with the induction of B. burgdorferi-specific antibodies, while the DNA-specific autoantibody responses mostly correlated in mice with a very high antibody response.
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: GPI-specific immune responses have been demonstrated to be causative for inflammatory arthritis in mouse models.
source: As GPI-specific immune responses have been demonstrated to be causative for inflammatory arthritis in mouse models and have been detected at least in subsets of human arthritis patients (Korganow et al., 1999; Monach et al., 2004), our findings may provide evidence for a direct link between the initial B. burgdorferi infection and the development of autoimmune arthritis occuring several years after the initial infection (Arvikar et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature (Korganow et al., 1999; Monach et al., 2004).

claim: GPI-specific immune responses have been detected at least in subsets of human arthritis patients.
source: As GPI-specific immune responses have been demonstrated to be causative for inflammatory arthritis in mouse models and have been detected at least in subsets of human arthritis patients (Korganow et al., 1999; Monach et al., 2004), our findings may provide evidence for a direct link between the initial B. burgdorferi infection and the development of autoimmune arthritis occuring several years after the initial infection (Arvikar et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature (Korganow et al., 1999; Monach et al., 2004).

claim: The findings may provide evidence for a direct link between the initial B. burgdorferi infection and the development of autoimmune arthritis occurring several years after the initial infection.
source: As GPI-specific immune responses have been demonstrated to be causative for inflammatory arthritis in mouse models and have been detected at least in subsets of human arthritis patients (Korganow et al., 1999; Monach et al., 2004), our findings may provide evidence for a direct link between the initial B. burgdorferi infection and the development of autoimmune arthritis occuring several years after the initial infection (Arvikar et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the observed correlation between pathogen-specific and autoreactive antibody responses and cited literature (Arvikar et al., 2017).

claim: The genetic background of individual HSC donors is different apart from the difference in FcγRIIb function.
source: First of all, apart from the difference in FcγRIIb function, the genetic background of the individual HSC donors is different.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge about the experimental design using HSC from different donors.

claim: Other genes impacting pathogen recognition, humoral tolerance or immune cell activation may contribute to the observed phenotypes.
source: Thus, it cannot be excluded that other genes impacting pathogen recognition, humoral tolerance or immune cell activation may contribute to the observed phenotypes.
evidence: The claim is speculative, acknowledging limitations of the experimental design.

claim: The human immune system in humanized mice has been developing only for three months.
source: A second major difference to a human patient population is that the human immune system in humanized mice has been developing only for three months.
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental protocol described in the methods.

claim: Not all immune cell subsets have reached their steady-state abundance in humanized mice.
source: Thus, not all immune cell subsets have reached their steady-state abundance, which is mirrored by the fact that B cells and IgM antibody responses dominate the immune response during this early developmental stage.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that the immune system is still developing in humanized mice.

claim: B cells and IgM antibody responses dominate the immune response during the early developmental stage in humanized mice.
source: Thus, not all immune cell subsets have reached their steady-state abundance, which is mirrored by the fact that B cells and IgM antibody responses dominate the immune response during this early developmental stage.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations of immune cell composition and antibody responses.

claim: The low level of IgG antibody responses may result in a more moderate disease pathology as only IgG antibodies are efficiently able to recruit FcγR-dependent effector pathways.
source: Especially the low level of IgG antibody responses may result in a more moderate disease pathology as only IgG antibodies are efficiently able to recruit FcγR-dependent effector pathways.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from established knowledge about IgG function and FcγR-dependent effector mechanisms.

claim: Humanized mice are kept under well-controlled conditions avoiding infections, which human patients will have encountered during their lifetime and which may alter consecutive immune responses.
source: Furthermore, humanized mice are kept under well-controlled conditions avoiding infections, which human patients will have encountered during their lifetime and which may alter consecutive immune responses.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge about animal husbandry practices and inference about potential effects on immune responses.

claim: The humoral immune response observed in humanized mice closely resembles at least in part the antibody response in humans.
source: Despite all these points to be considered, the fact that the humoral immune response observed in humanized mice closely resembles at least in part the antibody response in humans, underscores the value of this pre-clinical model system.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of antibody responses in humanized mice and human patients shown in Figures 1E, 5, and 6.

claim: The human inhibitory FcγRIIb is critical to limit self-reactive immune responses during the early phase of an infection with B. burgdorferi.
source: In summary, our study revealed that the human inhibitory FcγRIIb is critical to limit self-reactive immune responses during the early phase of an infection with B. burgdorferi.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined experimental results comparing humanized mice with functional and non-functional FcγRIIb alleles.

claim: A link between a primary infection with B. burgdorferi and the development of arthritis later in life has been suggested.
source: Considering that a link between a primary infection with B. burgdorferi and the development of arthritis later in life has been suggested it will be of great interest to study if humans with this non-functional FcγRIIb allele are more prone to develop arthritis, while they are more resistant to infection at the same time.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge from the literature.

claim: Loss of humoral tolerance has been associated with microbial infections.
source: While loss of humoral tolerance has been associated with microbial infections, the pathways involved in balancing protective versus autoreactive antibody responses in humans are incompletely understood.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge from the literature.

claim: Studies in classical mouse model systems have provided evidence that balancing of immune responses through inhibitory receptors is an important quality control checkpoint.
source: Studies in classical mouse model systems have provided evidence that balancing of immune responses through inhibitory receptors is an important quality control checkpoint.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge from the literature.

claim: Genetic differences between inbred mouse models and the outbred human population and allelic receptor variants not present in mice argue for caution when directly translating findings to the human system.
source: Genetic differences between inbred mouse models and the outbred human population and allelic receptor variants not present in mice; however, argue for caution when directly translating these findings to the human system.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about differences between mouse models and humans.

claim: The human inhibitory FcγRIIb is a critical checkpoint balancing protective and autoreactive immune responses, linking infection with induction of autoimmunity in the human immune system.
source: By studying Borrelia burgdorferi infection in humanized mice reconstituted with human hematopoietic stem cells from donors homozygous for a functional or a non-functional FcγRIIb allele, we show that the human inhibitory FcγRIIb is a critical checkpoint balancing protective and autoreactive immune responses, linking infection with induction of autoimmunity in the human immune system.
evidence: The claim is the main conclusion of the study, inferred from all experimental results.

claim: Loss of humoral tolerance is associated with the development of several severe autoimmune diseases, including rheumatoid arthritis and systemic lupus erythematosus.
source: Loss of humoral tolerance is associated with the development of several severe autoimmune diseases, including rheumatoid arthritis and systemic lupus erythematosus (Ludwig et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature (Ludwig et al., 2017).

claim: Autoantibodies can directly cause tissue inflammation and destruction.
source: A variety of well-defined inbred mouse model systems have firmly established that autoantibodies can directly cause tissue inflammation and destruction (Hogarth and Pietersz, 2012; Nimmerjahn and Ravetch, 2008; Takai, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature (Hogarth and Pietersz, 2012; Nimmerjahn and Ravetch, 2008; Takai, 2002).

claim: There is a link between infections and the induction of autoimmune diseases.
source: Of note, there is a link between infections and the induction of autoimmune diseases, suggesting that during the initiation of pathogen-specific immune responses self-reactive responses may be triggered (Brownlie et al., 2008; Smith and Clatworthy, 2010; Waisberg et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature (Brownlie et al., 2008; Smith and Clatworthy, 2010; Waisberg et al., 2011).

claim: An infection with Borrelia burgdorferi can lead to the development of joint inflammation and induction of autoimmune arthritis.
source: One prime example for such a scenario is an infection with Borrelia burgdorferi, which can lead to the development of joint inflammation and induction of autoimmune arthritis (Arvikar et al., 2017; Steere and Glickstein, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature (Arvikar et al., 2017; Steere and Glickstein, 2004).

claim: The inhibitory Fcγ-receptor IIb (FcγRIIb) expressed on B cells is one key factor for regulating humoral immune responses at several stages of B cell development.
source: Studies in inbred mouse model systems have identified the inhibitory Fcγ-receptor IIb (FcγRIIb) expressed on B cells as one key factor for regulating humoral immune responses at several stages of B cell development (Daëron et al., 1995; Smith and Clatworthy, 2010; Takai, 2002; Tarasenko et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature (Daëron et al., 1995; Smith and Clatworthy, 2010; Takai, 2002; Tarasenko et al., 2007).

claim: Mice with altered FcγRIIb expression or a B-cell-specific/ubiquitous deletion of FcγRIIb show higher levels of IgM and IgG antibody responses, have an impaired germinal center reaction, and develop a systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) like disease on susceptible genetic backgrounds.
source: Mice with altered FcγRIIb expression or a B-cell-specific/ubiquitous deletion of FcγRIIb show higher levels of IgM and IgG antibody responses, have an impaired germinal center reaction, and develop a systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) like disease on susceptible genetic backgrounds (Bolland and Ravetch, 2000; Bolland et al., 2002; Espéli et al., 2012; Li et al., 2014; Su et al., 2004a; Su et al., 2004b; Takai et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature (Bolland and Ravetch, 2000; Bolland et al., 2002; Espéli et al., 2012; Li et al., 2014; Su et al., 2004a; Su et al., 2004b; Takai et al., 1996).

claim: Mice with a general or a B-cell-specific overexpression of FcγRIIb showed reduced autoantibody production and autoimmune disease development.
source: In contrast, mice with a general or a B-cell-specific overexpression of FcγRIIb showed reduced autoantibody production and autoimmune disease development (Brownlie et al., 2008; McGaha et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature (Brownlie et al., 2008; McGaha et al., 2005).

claim: Mice generated on the C57BL/6 background developed a less pronounced autoimmune phenotype, suggesting that other genes act in concert with FcγRIIb to break humoral tolerance in mice.
source: As mice generated on the C57BL/6 background developed a less pronounced autoimmune phenotype it was suggested that other genes act in concert with FcγRIIb to break humoral tolerance in mice (Boross et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature (Boross et al., 2011).

claim: Isolated triggering of FcγRIIb on plasma cells induces apoptosis.
source: Apart from regulating the level and quality of antibody responses, isolated triggering of FcγRIIb on plasma cells was shown to induce apoptosis, suggesting that FcγRIIb may also regulate plasma cell homeostasis (Xiang et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature (Xiang et al., 2007).

claim: FcγRIIb may regulate plasma cell homeostasis.
source: Apart from regulating the level and quality of antibody responses, isolated triggering of FcγRIIb on plasma cells was shown to induce apoptosis, suggesting that FcγRIIb may also regulate plasma cell homeostasis (Xiang et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from cited literature (Xiang et al., 2007).

claim: The level of inhibitory Fcγ-receptor IIb expression correlated with the development and severity of several autoimmune diseases in humans.
source: In humans, the level of inhibitory Fcγ-receptor IIb expression correlated with the development and severity of several autoimmune diseases.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge from the literature.

claim: Patients with SLE and chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy express lower levels of FcγRIIb on mature B cells and fail to upregulate FcγRIIb expression on memory B cells.
source: Patients with SLE and chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy, for example, were shown to express lower levels of FcγRIIb on mature B cells and failed to upregulate FcγRIIb expression on memory B cells (Mackay et al., 2006; Tackenberg et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature (Mackay et al., 2006; Tackenberg et al., 2009).

claim: Polymorphisms in the fcgr2b promoter and in the FcγRIIb transmembrane domain have been associated with the development of SLE.
source: Moreover, polymorphisms in the fcgr2b promoter and in the FcγRIIb transmembrane domain have been associated with the development of SLE (Floto et al., 2005; Kono et al., 2005; Niederer et al., 2010; Su et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature (Floto et al., 2005; Kono et al., 2005; Niederer et al., 2010; Su et al., 2007).

claim: The human FcγRIIb-232T allele results in an altered plasma membrane localization and decreased receptor function.
source: Interestingly, the human FcγRIIb-232T allele, in which an isoleucine residue in the transmembrane domain of the receptor is replaced with a threonine residue, resulting in an altered plasma membrane localization and decreased receptor function, was shown to be enriched in areas with malaria (Clatworthy et al., 2007; Waisberg et al., 2011; Willcocks et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature (Clatworthy et al., 2007; Waisberg et al., 2011; Willcocks et al., 2010).

claim: The human FcγRIIb-232T allele was shown to be enriched in areas with malaria.
source: Interestingly, the human FcγRIIb-232T allele, in which an isoleucine residue in the transmembrane domain of the receptor is replaced with a threonine residue, resulting in an altered plasma membrane localization and decreased receptor function, was shown to be enriched in areas with malaria (Clatworthy et al., 2007; Waisberg et al., 2011; Willcocks et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature (Clatworthy et al., 2007; Waisberg et al., 2011; Willcocks et al., 2010).

claim: Under negative selection pressure, a decreased level of FcγRIIb expression may provide a competitive advantage for mounting faster parasite-specific immune responses at the potential risk of inducing autoimmunity.
source: Thus, under negative selection pressure, a decreased level of FcγRIIb expression may provide a competitive advantage for mounting faster parasite-specific immune responses at the potential risk of inducing autoimmunity.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the enrichment of the FcγRIIb-232T allele in malaria-endemic regions.

claim: FcγRIIb is expressed on human dendritic cells present in the spleen of humanized mice.
source: Indeed, FcγRIIb is also expressed on human dendritic cells (DC) present in the spleen of humanized mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.
